title: ITA Section 248(1): SR&ED Statutory Definitions Guide
description: Learn the foundational criteria for Canadian R&D claims under ITA Section 248(1) legislation, which sets out the official SR&ED statutory definitions.
summary: Subsection 248(1) of Canada's Income Tax Act defines scientific research and experimental development (SR&ED) as a systematic investigation in science or technology, by experiment or analysis, covering basic research, applied research and experimental development. Canadian claimants must meet this definition before any expenditure qualifies for the federal SR&ED deduction and investment tax credits of 15% to 35%.

body.text: Subsection 248(1) of Canada's Income Tax Act defines scientific research and experimental development (SR&ED) as a systematic investigation in science or technology, by experiment or analysis, covering basic research, applied research and experimental development. Canadian claimants must meet this definition before any expenditure qualifies for the federal SR&ED deduction and investment tax credits of 15% to 35%.
Executive Summary and Statutory Architecture of Canadian R&D Incentives

Canada maintains one of the most mature and generously funded statutory research and development (R&D) tax incentive frameworks among industrialized economies. Anchored federally by the Scientific Research and Experimental Development (SR&ED) Tax Incentive Program, the regime operates as a dual-mechanism fiscal incentive enacted under the federal Income Tax Act (ITA) and the Income Tax Regulations (ITR). The program provides performing taxpayers with two distinct, interlocking statutory benefits: first, an immediate 100% income tax deduction—or indefinite pool carryforward—for allowable SR&ED expenditures under subsection 37(1) of the ITA; and second, an Investment Tax Credit (ITC) ranging from a basic rate of 15% to an enhanced rate of 35% on qualified SR&ED expenditures under section 127 and section 127.1 of the ITA.

Between December 2024 and March 2026, the Canadian R&D tax landscape underwent its most consequential structural modernization since the 2012 federal budget reforms. Announced in the 2024 Fall Economic Statement, articulated in the Department of Finance's August 2025 legislative proposals, expanded in Budget 2025 (tabled November 4, 2025), and enacted through Bill C-15 (Budget 2025 Implementation Act, No. 1), which received Royal Assent on March 26, 2026, the federal government reversed over a decade of base-narrowing policies. Specifically, Parliament restored the eligibility of SR&ED capital expenditures and lease costs incurred after December 15, 2024, expanded access to the enhanced 35% ITC rate to include Eligible Canadian Public Corporations (ECPCs) alongside Canadian-controlled private corporations (CCPCs), elevated the annual expenditure limit for the 35% ITC from $3 million to $6 million (following an interim draft legislative proposal of $4.5 million), and widened the prior-year taxable capital phase-out thresholds from the historic $10 million–$50 million corridor to a substantially broader $15 million–$75 million range.

Concurrently, provincial jurisdictions executed major structural realignments to complement the federal overhaul. Most notably, Quebec's 2025 Budget dismantled eight legacy fragmented R&D tax credits for taxation years beginning after March 25, 2025, consolidating them into the size-neutral, fully refundable Crédit d'impôt pour la recherche, l'innovation et la commercialisation (CRIC), which offers a 30% rate on the first $1 million of eligible R&D and pre-commercialization spending above an exclusion threshold and 20% on the excess, while transitioning its flagship information technology salary credit into an artificial-intelligence-focused incentive (CDAEIA) effective for fiscal years starting after December 31, 2025. Saskatchewan similarly doubled the annual qualifying expenditure limit for its 10% refundable R&D tax credit for CCPCs from $1 million to $2 million for expenditures after December 15, 2024 and extended the credit to eligible capital expenditures. When federal SR&ED incentives are stacked with provincial tax credits across jurisdictions such as Quebec, Ontario, Alberta, British Columbia, and Atlantic Canada, qualifying corporations can recover between 40% and 65% of their gross R&D outlays, subject to statutory government assistance grind-down interactions under paragraph 37(1)(d) and subsection 127(18) of the ITA.
Federal SR&ED Legislative Framework and 2024–2026 Statutory Reforms
The Dual-Pillar Statutory Mechanism: Section 37 Pooling and Section 127 Investment Tax Credits

The legal architecture of the federal SR&ED program is bifurcated into expenditure deductibility and tax credit generation, with tax policy formulated by the Department of Finance Canada and operational administration carried out by the Canada Revenue Agency (CRA). Under the first statutory pillar, subsection 37(1) of the ITA establishes a dedicated notional pool of deductible SR&ED expenditures. Unlike ordinary commercial operating expenses—which are governed by general income computation principles and must be deducted in the fiscal period incurred—allowable SR&ED expenditures pooled under subsection 37(1) may be deducted in whole or in part to reduce taxable income in the current taxation year, or carried forward indefinitely to offset taxable income in any future taxation year. Pursuant to paragraph 37(1)(d) of the ITA, this deductible expenditure pool must be reduced by any government assistance, non-government assistance, or contract payments that the claimant has received, is entitled to receive, or can reasonably be expected to receive in respect of the SR&ED. Furthermore, any federal SR&ED ITC claimed or refunded in a given taxation year reduces the subsection 37(1) pool balance in the subsequent taxation year, preventing a duplicative tax benefit on the same dollar of expenditure.

Under the second statutory pillar, section 127 and section 127.1 of the ITA govern the calculation, application, carryback, carryforward, and refundability of SR&ED Investment Tax Credits. The rate of ITC earned and the proportion of that credit eligible for a cash refund depend on the legal classification of the claimant, the nature of the expenditure as current or capital, and the corporation's prior-year taxable capital employed in Canada or three-year average annual revenue.

body.text: Expansion of the 35% Enhanced ITC Rate to Eligible Canadian Public Corporations (ECPCs)

Historically, Canada's two-tier SR&ED rate structure created a severe fiscal cliff whenever an innovative domestic technology or life sciences company executed an initial public offering or became controlled by a public parent entity. Under the pre-December 16, 2024 framework, only a Canadian-controlled private corporation (CCPC) as defined in subsection 125(7) of the ITA qualified for the additional 20% ITC under subsection 127(10.1), bringing its total credit rate to 35%. Upon listing on a public stock exchange, a Canadian company immediately ceased to be a CCPC, causing its SR&ED ITC rate to plummet from a 100% refundable 35% credit to a non-refundable 15% basic credit.

To eliminate this structural disincentive to domestic public capitalization and scale-up retention, the legislative amendments in Bill C-15, which received Royal Assent on March 26, 2026, amended subsection 127(10.1) and enacted new subsection 127(10.6) of the ITA, applicable to taxation years beginning on or after December 16, 2024. Under these enacted provisions, a corporation that qualifies as an Eligible Canadian Public Corporation (ECPC) throughout the taxation year is entitled to earn the enhanced 35% ITC rate on qualified SR&ED expenditures up to its annual expenditure limit.
Expenditure Limit Formulas, Phase-Out Mechanics, and Associated Group Rules

For taxation years beginning before December 16, 2024, a CCPC's maximum expenditure limit for the 35% enhanced rate was fixed at $3,000,000, shared across all associated corporations. That $3,000,000 limit phased out gradually where the associated group's taxable capital employed in Canada—a statutory concept defined in the ITA and further explained in archived Interpretation Bulletin IT-532 (Part I.3 – Tax on Large Corporations)—in the preceding taxation year fell between $10,000,000 and $50,000,000. In earlier taxation years (specifically for the 2010 and subsequent pre-reform taxation years), the expenditure limit was also constrained by a qualifying income limit formula based on prior-year taxable income exceeding $500,000 and phasing out completely when previous-year taxable income exceeded $800,000 (having previously been increased from an earlier $300,000 to $500,000 range). Under that historical formula, the qualifying income limit of a corporation was calculated as follows.

In this expression, B equalled nil if the prior-year taxable capital amount was less than or equal to $10,000,000, or the lesser of $40,000,000 and the amount by which the taxable capital amount exceeded $10,000,000 in any other case. Following the elimination of the taxable income phase-out, only the prior-year taxable capital phase-out remained active for CCPCs prior to the December 2024 reforms.

For taxation years beginning after December 15, 2024, the statutory expenditure limit and phase-out architecture operate under two parallel methodologies depending on whether the claimant is a CCPC or an ECPC. Under the expanded taxable capital method for CCPCs governed by subsection 127(10.2) of the ITA, the maximum annual expenditure limit is increased to $6,000,000 by Bill C-15, as reflected in the CRA's updated SR&ED Investment Tax Credit Policy, building upon the $4,500,000 limit originally articulated in the August 2025 draft legislative proposals. Simultaneously, the prior-year taxable capital phase-out thresholds are widened so that the expenditure limit begins to decrease only once previous-year taxable capital employed in Canada reaches $15,000,000 and is completely phased out at $75,000,000. Expressed mathematically, for a CCPC group with prior-year taxable capital (K) between $15,000,000 and $75,000,000, the unprorated expenditure limit (E) scales down across the $60,000,000 phase-out span:

Under the alternative three-year average annual revenue method governed by subsections 127(10.6) to 127(10.64) of the ITA, an ECPC's expenditure limit is determined by a statutory formula that reduces the limit based on the average annual revenue reflected in the financial statements of the corporation—and of each corporation that is a member of a consolidated ECPC group—over the preceding three fiscal years, with the limit starting to decrease when average annual revenue reaches $15,000,000 and becoming nil at $75,000,000 or more. Crucially, for taxation years beginning after December 15, 2024, CCPCs may formally elect under subsection 127(10.31) (or, for an associated group, jointly under subsection 127(10.32)) using the prescribed form to dispense with the subsection 127(10.2) taxable capital test and instead compute their expenditure limit using the ECPC three-year average annual revenue method. Where an associated CCPC group makes this election for a taxation year, the expenditure limit based on taxable capital employed in Canada under subsection 127(10.2) does not apply to the group for that year. This election provides critical structural relief to capital-intensive private corporations—such as biotechnology, clean-technology, and hardware enterprises—that accumulate substantial debt or equity capital on their balance sheets exceeding $15 million while generating minimal commercial revenue during extended research phases.

Special proration rules apply where a corporation has a short taxation year, or where a CCPC has more than one taxation year ending in the same calendar year while associated in two or more of those taxation years with another CCPC that has a taxation year ending in that same calendar year. Pursuant to subsection 127(10.5) of the ITA (which was renumbered from former subsection 127(10.6) effective for taxation years beginning on or after December 16, 2024), the corporation's allocated expenditure limit for the short taxation year must be prorated by the number of days in the short taxation year relative to 365 days. For example, as illustrated in the CRA's SR&ED Investment Tax Credit Policy, where Corporation P and Corporation Q are associated CCPCs that have been allocated $3,000,000 of the group expenditure limit each, and Corporation P has a June 30, 2027 tax year-end followed by a change of year-end to December 31, 2027 (creating a second tax year of 184 days from July 1 to December 31, 2027 in the same calendar year as Corporation Q's December 31, 2027 year-end), Corporation P's expenditure limit for its December 31, 2027 tax year-end is determined under subsection 127(10.5) as:
Refundability, Carryback, and Carryforward Rules

Under section 127.1 of the ITA, SR&ED ITCs that exceed a taxpayer's Part I federal income tax otherwise payable may be refunded in cash depending on the claimant's classification and whether the underlying expenditures are of a current or capital nature. Pursuant to subsections 127.1(2) and 127.1(2.01) of the ITA, a CCPC—including a CCPC that is neither a "qualifying corporation" nor an "excluded corporation" as defined in subsection 127.1(2)—is entitled to a 100% rate of refund on the 35% enhanced ITC earned in respect of qualified SR&ED expenditures of a current nature. Conversely, for restored SR&ED expenditures of a capital nature (incurred in respect of property acquired on or after December 16, 2024 and eligible lease costs first becoming payable on or after December 16, 2024), the definition of "refundable investment tax credit" and subsection 127.1(2.01) establish a 40% rate of refund on the ITC earned.

Claimants that do not qualify for the enhanced 35% rate—including non-CCPC and non-ECPC corporations, large corporations phased out of the expenditure limit, sole proprietorships (individuals), partners of a partnership, and beneficiaries of trusts—earn ITCs at the basic rate of 15% on qualified SR&ED expenditures. For corporations earning the 15% basic rate outside the CCPC refundability provisions, the ITC is non-refundable and may only be applied to reduce Part I tax otherwise payable. Unused ITC balances may be carried back up to 3 taxation years or carried forward up to 20 taxation years (following transitional rules that previously allowed 1998 credits to be carried forward to 2018). When carrying back an ITC to any of the 3 preceding taxation years, the carryback allowed to a prior year is strictly limited to the amount by which Part I tax otherwise payable in that prior year exceeds the ITC already available and applied in that prior year. For example, if a claimant had $10,000 of Part I tax otherwise payable and $6,000 of ITC available in Year 1 (leaving $4,000 of net Part I tax), and in Year 2 has $12,000 of Part I tax otherwise payable and $15,000 of current-year ITC available (resulting in $3,000 of excess ITC in Year 2), the ITC allowed for carryback to Year 1 is limited to $3,000. Any ITC that is not applied to reduce Part I tax otherwise payable within the 20-year carryforward period expires permanently.
Qualifying SR&ED Expenditures (QREs), Overhead Methodologies, and Capital Cost Restoration
Salaries and Wages and Specified Employee Restrictions

Salaries and wages paid to employees who directly undertake, supervise, or support the performance of SR&ED constitute the foundational expenditure category for most Canadian claimants. Under subsection 78(4) of the ITA and the CRA SR&ED Salary or Wages Policy, eligible salary or wages must be incurred in the taxation year and actually paid inside the taxation year or within 180 days of the taxation year-end. Any unpaid remuneration that remains outstanding after the 180-day window cannot be included in the current year's SR&ED claim and is excluded from the proxy salary base even when paid in a subsequent taxation year. Furthermore, for all employees—whether specified employees or arm's-length staff—the salary base cannot include taxable benefits under section 6 of the ITA, stock option benefits under section 7 of the ITA, bonuses, or remuneration based on profits.

Stricter statutory limits govern "specified employees"—individuals who do not deal at arm's length with the claimant or who own, directly or indirectly, 10% or more of the issued shares of any class of the corporation or a related corporation. When computing the salary base for the Prescribed Proxy Amount (PPA) under the proxy method, subsection 2900(7) of the ITR restricts the maximum amount that a claimant can include for a specified employee to the lesser of two statutory ceilings. The first ceiling is 75% of the specified employee's total salary or wages across both SR&ED and non-SR&ED duties, strictly excluding bonuses, remuneration based on profits, section 6 taxable benefits, and prior-year unpaid salary or wages paid in the year. The second ceiling is 2.5 times the Year's Maximum Pensionable Earnings (YMPE, determined annually for purposes of the Canada Pension Plan) for the calendar year in which the claimant's taxation year ends, prorated by the number of days of employment in the taxation year according to the statutory formula:

In this formula, A represents the YMPE for the calendar year in which the taxation year ends, and B represents the number of days in the taxation year that the claimant employed the individual, with no proration for any portion of the year during which the employee was not a specified employee. Where a specified employee of a corporation is also employed by one or more associated corporations, additional allocation rules under section 4.2 of the CRA Prescribed Proxy Amount Policy constrain the aggregate salary base across the associated group.
Overhead Calculation Methodologies: Traditional Method vs. Proxy Method (PPA)

To account for SR&ED overhead and indirect support costs, claimants must choose between the Traditional Method and the Proxy Method for each taxation year. Under the Traditional Method, the claimant tracks and substantiates actual overhead and other expenditures directly related and incremental to the prosecution of SR&ED, as well as the salaries or wages of indirect support employees who are not directly engaged in hands-on SR&ED. Those actual overhead expenditures are added to the subsection 37(1) pool of deductible SR&ED expenditures and also earn SR&ED ITCs under section 127.

Conversely, when a claimant elects to use the Proxy Method, the claimant does not track or claim actual SR&ED overhead expenditures or indirect support wages on Form T661. Instead, the claimant calculates a notional Prescribed Proxy Amount (PPA) under subsection 2900(4) of the ITR as a percentage of the eligible salary base. Following the 2012 federal budget—which reduced the proxy rate from 65% for 2012 and prior years to 60% for 2013—the PPA has been fixed since January 1, 2014 at 55% of the salary base. The salary base for the proxy method is composed exclusively of the eligible salaries and wages of employees who are directly engaged in SR&ED (reported on lines 300 and 307 of Form T661), subject to the exclusions in subsection 2900(9) and the specified employee restrictions in subsection 2900(7) of the ITR. Under subsection 2900(5) of the ITR, if an employee is directly engaged in SR&ED for all or substantially all (ASA)—defined as 90% or more—of their employment time, 100% of their eligible salary (subject to specified employee caps) qualifies for inclusion in the salary base.

Because the PPA is a purely notional amount used in lieu of actual SR&ED overhead and other expenditures when calculating qualified SR&ED expenditures to earn the SR&ED ITC, the PPA is never included in the subsection 37(1) pool of deductible SR&ED expenditures. Instead, the actual overhead expenses that the PPA represents are deducted as ordinary business expenses outside the SR&ED pool, while the notional 55% PPA generates SR&ED ITCs (subject to an overall cap on the PPA where applicable).

body.text: The structural divergence between the Traditional Method and the Proxy Method is demonstrated in Section 6.10 of the CRA's Traditional and Proxy Methods Policy. Where a CCPC incurs $100,000 in directly engaged SR&ED salaries, $15,000 in eligible materials, and $50,000 in actual SR&ED overhead, electing the Traditional Method yields $165,000 of allowable SR&ED expenditures in the subsection 37(1) pool, $0 of PPA, $165,000 of total qualified SR&ED expenditures, and a 35% ITC of $57,750. Electing the Proxy Method on the identical cost structure yields $115,000 of allowable SR&ED expenditures in the subsection 37(1) pool (with the $50,000 of overhead deducted separately outside the pool), a notional PPA of $55,000 ($100,000 salary base multiplied by 55%), total qualified SR&ED expenditures of $170,000, and a higher 35% ITC of $59,500.
Materials Consumed or Transformed, Subcontractors, and Third-Party Payments

Under both the Traditional and Proxy methods, claimants may claim expenditures for materials that are either consumed or transformed in performing SR&ED in Canada. As mandated by the 2012 federal budget reforms and the CRA Materials Policy, an expenditure of a capital nature can never be claimed as an expenditure for materials for SR&ED. Furthermore, where SR&ED is conducted alongside or within commercial production facilities, any production beyond what is strictly required for the experimental investigation is classified as ineligible excess production.

When a claimant engages an arm's-length contractor or subcontractor to perform SR&ED work directly on the claimant's behalf, or makes third-party payments to approved research entities (including transactions made by agricultural organizations, which constitute transactions made by producers under section 8.0 of the CRA Third-Party Payments Policy), 100% of the eligible contract outlay is deductible in the subsection 37(1) pool, but only 80% of the expenditure is eligible to earn SR&ED ITCs. This 80% inclusion fraction—which took effect after 2012—applies identically under both the Traditional Method and the Proxy Method. Where SR&ED is performed between non-arm's-length parties and qualified expenditures are transferred by agreement, the performer must report the agreed transferred amount on line 540 of Form T661.
The December 16, 2024 Restoration of SR&ED Capital Expenditures and Shared-Use Equipment

Following the 2012 federal budget, capital expenditures (including shared-use equipment) and equipment lease costs were completely eliminated from the SR&ED program effective January 1, 2014. To revitalize capital investment in physical laboratories, pilot plants, and advanced hardware research, the federal government restored SR&ED capital expenditures and lease costs for property acquired on or after December 16, 2024 (after December 15, 2024) and lease payments that first become payable on or after December 16, 2024. Enacted through amendments to subsections 37(6), 37(8)(a)(ii)(B)(II), 37(8)(e), 127(11.5), and 127.1 of the ITA (enacted by Bill C-15, which received Royal Assent on March 26, 2026), the restored capital regime covers wholly dedicated SR&ED equipment, shared-use equipment, and leased equipment.

For wholly dedicated capital assets, an SR&ED capital expenditure is an outlay made to acquire new or used depreciable property (acquired and available for use after December 15, 2024) that the claimant intended either to use all or substantially all (ASA, meaning 90% or more) of the operating time in its expected useful life to perform SR&ED in Canada, or to consume ASA (90% or more) of its value to perform SR&ED in Canada. Non-depreciable property such as land is excluded, and buildings remain generally excluded under section 37. Claimants report these dedicated capital expenditures on line 390 of Form T661 and must enter the names of the 10 most expensive SR&ED properties acquired after December 15, 2024 used in each project on lines 262 and 263 of Form T661.

Where newly acquired equipment does not meet the 90% ASA criterion because it is shared between SR&ED and commercial activities, it may qualify as Shared-Use Equipment (SUE) on line 504 of Form T661. To qualify as first-term shared-use equipment, the asset must be depreciable property acquired after December 15, 2024, must not be prescribed depreciable property (PDP) or general purpose office equipment or furniture (GPOEF), and must be used by the claimant during its operating time—in the period starting when the equipment was acquired and available for use and ending at the end of the first taxation year that is at least 12 months after that time—primarily for the prosecution of SR&ED in Canada. For SR&ED purposes, the term "primarily" is defined strictly as more than 50% but less than 90%. If the equipment satisfies the requirements of both first-term SUE and second-term SUE, the claimant claims 25% of the capital cost of the equipment on line 504 in the first period (first-term SUE) and another 25% of the capital cost in the second period (second-term SUE).

Lease costs for the right to use equipment in SR&ED also qualify to the extent that the lease payments first become payable on or after December 16, 2024, provided that claimants electing the proxy method do not include lease costs for general purpose office equipment or furniture (GPOEF). If a claimant's taxation year began before December 16, 2024 and straddles the transition date, the claimant must calculate SR&ED use as a percentage of total operating time strictly for the period after December 15, 2024, and must exclude all expenditures, provincial/territorial government assistance (line 514), non-arm's-length outlays (line 535), and transferred expenditures (line 540) relating to depreciable property acquired or lease costs incurred before December 16, 2024. Additionally, if property on which an SR&ED ITC was claimed is subsequently disposed of or converted to commercial use, ITC recapture provisions apply to recover the credit.
Technological Eligibility Criteria, Judicial Precedents, and CRA Audit Administration
Statutory Definition of SR&ED under Subsection 248(1)

Regardless of accounting classification, no expenditure qualifies for SR&ED tax incentives unless the underlying scientific or engineering work meets the statutory definition of "scientific research and experimental development" in subsection 248(1) of the ITA. Subsection 248(1) requires a systematic investigation or search carried out in a field of science or technology by means of experiment or analysis, encompassing basic research (undertaken for the advancement of scientific knowledge without a specific practical application in view), applied research (undertaken for the advancement of scientific knowledge with a specific practical application in view), and experimental development (undertaken for the purpose of achieving technological advancement to create new, or improve existing, materials, devices, products, or processes), along with commensurate engineering, design, mathematical analysis, computer programming, data collection, and testing directly in support of that research. Conversely, routine commercial activities such as sales promotion—defined as work that supplements advertising and personal selling—routine quality control, and standard product development using known procedures are statutorily excluded.
The Five-Question Judicial Framework: Northwest Hydraulic and Subsequent Jurisprudence

Both the CRA's administrative eligibility guidelines and Canadian tax litigation are anchored in the landmark Tax Court of Canada decision of Judge Donald Bowman (later Chief Justice of the Tax Court of Canada) in Northwest Hydraulic Consultants Limited v. The Queen, 98 D.T.C. 1839, [1998] 3 C.T.C. 2520 (TCC), whose analytical framework was formally adopted by the Federal Court of Appeal in C.W. Agencies Inc. v. The Queen (also cited as CW Agencies Inc. v. Canada), 2001 FCA 393. As summarized by Justice Russell in Clevor Technologies Inc. v. Her Majesty the Queen, 2019 TCC 166 (at paragraph 11) and applied in Joel Theatrical Rigging Contractors (1980) Ltd., Emotion Picture Studios Inc., and Manning Canning Kitchens Inc. v. His Majesty the King (2025), the jurisprudence establishes five cumulative questions to determine whether activities constitute SR&ED under subsection 248(1):

items: Was there a technological risk or uncertainty which could not be removed by routine engineering or standard procedures?
Did the person claiming to be doing SR&ED formulate hypotheses specifically aimed at reducing or eliminating that technological uncertainty?
Did the procedure adopted accord with the total discipline of the scientific method including the formulation, testing, and modification of the hypotheses?
Did the process result in a technological advancement?
Was a detailed record of the hypotheses tested and results kept as the work progressed?

body.text: In applying the first question regarding technological uncertainty, the Tax Court of Canada in Manning Canning Kitchens Inc. v. His Majesty the King (at paragraphs 9–14) emphasized that merely facing an uncertain path toward a commercial objective—or not knowing at the outset of a project the exact steps required to meet a product development challenge—is not, in and of itself, sufficient to qualify a project as SR&ED. Rather, the taxpayer bears the legal burden of proving, on a balance of probabilities, that the technical risk or uncertainty could not be resolved through routine engineering or standard procedures. Technological uncertainty may also manifest as system uncertainty where individual components are known but their interaction behaves unpredictably. Under the fourth question regarding technological advancement, Judge Bowman held in Northwest Hydraulic (as cited at paragraph 27 of Manning Canning) that the criterion may be answered in the affirmative if the experimental process resulted in an advancement of general scientific or technological understanding, even if the specific commercial product objective was not achieved.
Judicial Clarifications on Contemporaneous Documentation and Expert Witness Testimony

While CRA Research and Technology Advisors (RTAs) rely on the five questions and the documentation tools in the Claim Review Manual for Research and Technology Advisors to evaluate claims during audits, the Tax Court of Canada has established critical legal protections regarding the fifth question on contemporaneous documentation and the proper scope of expert testimony. In 116736 Canada inc. v. Canada, [1998] A.C.I. No. 478 (QL), Justice Archambault explained that although contemporary reports showing detailed records of each experiment attempted by a researcher are potentially very important evidence of a systematic investigation—and a taxpayer attempting to convince the Minister or the Court without such written evidence places themselves in a very precarious position—the Income Tax Act and the Income Tax Regulations do not require that written reports be produced in order for a taxpayer to qualify for SR&ED deductions. Instead, a taxpayer may adduce evidence by way of oral testimony, reducing the issue to a question of witness credibility.

This principle was forcefully reaffirmed by Justice Jorré in Les Abeilles Service de Conditionnement Inc. v. The Queen, where the Tax Court allowed the taxpayer's appeal after finding that the work was undertaken to achieve technological advancement and did not involve routine procedures. Justice Jorré held that while the existence and content of contemporaneous documents are relevant to determining questions of fact, the existence of contemporaneous documentation—or contemporaneous documents with specific content—is not a legal condition for SR&ED to be recognized, noting that in tax matters, taxpayers cannot be required to do more than the obligations the Act imposes on them. Furthermore, Les Abeilles established two vital procedural precedents for SR&ED litigation: first, under paragraph 153 of the decision, each project must be considered globally over the year rather than dissecting each test individually in isolation; and second, when a CRA scientific adviser who participated in the audit testifies as an expert witness before the Tax Court, they must base their testimony on their own independent personal expertise regarding technological uncertainty rather than merely applying CRA administrative guidelines and internal audit proof standards.
Filing Procedures, Statutory Deadlines, and Administrative Penalties

To claim federal SR&ED tax incentives, claimants must complete Form T661 (Scientific Research and Experimental Development (SR&ED) Expenditures Claim) in accordance with CRA Guide T4088, alongside Schedule T2SCH31 for corporations. The statutory filing deadline for submitting Form T661 and the accompanying ITC schedule is 12 months after the taxpayer's income tax return filing due date—which for a corporation equates to a strict 18-month filing window from the end of the taxation year in which the eligible expenditures were incurred. In addition, claimants and third-party claim preparers (including consultants charging on a contingency-fee basis) are subject to strict compliance oversight; where a claimant overstates an SR&ED claim—such as by claiming normal commercial salaries as SR&ED—under circumstances amounting to gross negligence, the CRA assesses civil penalties under the gross negligence penalty provisions of the ITA.
Provincial and Territorial R&D Tax Credit Regimes and Recent Reforms

In addition to the federal SR&ED program, Canadian provinces and Yukon provide substantial regional R&D tax credits and tax-system grants that stack onto federal incentives. While Revenu Québec administers Quebec's R&D and IT tax credits via the CO-17 corporate tax return and Alberta administers its Innovation Employment Grant through the Alberta corporate tax system (AT1 Schedule 29), the CRA administers the provincial and territorial R&D tax credits for Ontario, British Columbia, Saskatchewan, Manitoba, Nova Scotia, New Brunswick, Newfoundland and Labrador, and Yukon.

body.text: Quebec's 2025–2026 Paradigm Shift: The CRIC Revolution and CDAEIA Transition

For taxation years and partnership fiscal periods beginning on or before March 25, 2025, Quebec operated a fragmented system of eight R&D tax measures led by the refundable Tax Credit for Salaries and Wages (R&D), filed on Form TP-1029.8.6-V with the CO-17 corporate income tax return within 18 months of fiscal year-end. Under that legacy credit, SMEs with consolidated assets under $75 million and prior-year gross revenue under $50 million earned a 30% refundable credit, which phased down to a 14% base rate for large corporations, calculated on 100% of Quebec R&D salaries and 50% of arm's-length subcontractor costs above an exclusion threshold ($50,000 for SMEs up to $225,000 for large businesses). Separate legacy credits provided 30% (SME) or 14% (large business) on 80% of university or public research centre R&D contracts, 100% of current expenses and 80% of subcontracts for private partnership pre-competitive research, and 100% of research consortium dues, alongside specialized credits for technological adaptation services, industrial design (24% SME / 12% large business), and foreign researcher/expert tax holidays.

In the 2025 Quebec Budget, the provincial government overhauled this architecture for taxation years and partnership fiscal periods beginning after March 25, 2025 by eliminating the tax credit for R&D salaries and wages, the tax credit for university or public research centre research, the tax credit for private partnership pre-competitive research, the tax credit for fees and dues paid to a research consortium, and the tax credit for technological adaptation services (while removing industrial design from the outside-consultant and in-house design credits), consolidating them into the new refundable Tax Credit for Research, Innovation and Commercialization (Crédit d'impôt pour la recherche, l'innovation et la commercialisation — CRIC). Unlike the legacy regime, the CRIC applies a universal, size-neutral two-tier rate structure to startups, SMEs, and large multinational corporations alike: a 30% fully refundable tax credit on the first $1,000,000 of eligible expenditures in excess of an exclusion threshold, and a 20% fully refundable tax credit on all eligible expenditures exceeding that $1,000,000 limit.

Crucially, the CRIC expands Quebec's qualifying expenditure base beyond traditional federal SR&ED in two major respects. First, it covers pre-commercialization activities—such as product design continuing R&D activities in Quebec, regulatory testing, and market validation—that bridge the gap between resolving technological uncertainty and commercial launch. Second, it includes capital expenditures for the acquisition of depreciable property (such as laboratory, testing, and prototyping equipment) used in Quebec R&D and pre-commercialization, alongside eligible salaries and wages, 50% of arm's-length subcontractor contracts, and payments to certain research organizations. Under the CRIC, the exclusion threshold corresponds to the greater of $50,000 and the sum, for each employee, of the basic personal amount under the Quebec personal income tax plan ($18,571 in 2025), adjusted in proportion to the time each employee spends on eligible R&D and pre-commercialization activities. Separately, Quebec businesses investing in manufacturing equipment, computer hardware, and management software above $5,000 or $12,500 per property can claim the fully refundable C3i tax credit at rates of 15%, 20%, or 25% depending on regional economic vitality, up to a cumulative $100 million cap over four years.

In parallel, Quebec restructured its e-business IT salary credit. For fiscal years starting on or before December 31, 2025, the Crédit d'impôt pour le développement des affaires électroniques (CDAE) provides a 30% credit on eligible IT employee salaries capped at $83,333 per employee per year (where the employee spends at least 75% of their time on eligible IT tasks and the corporation obtains an annual certificate from Investissement Québec, which charges application analysis fees). The 30% CDAE rate is split into 24% refundable and 6% non-refundable for fiscal years starting in 2024, and 23% refundable and 7% non-refundable for fiscal years starting in 2025. For fiscal years starting after December 31, 2025, the CDAE is replaced by the CDAEIA, which requires that qualifying corporations integrate artificial intelligence (AI) features in a significant way and calculates the 30% credit on eligible salary above an exclusion threshold (halved in certain non-arm's-length cases), with the refundable versus non-refundable split shifting to 22% refundable / 8% non-refundable in 2026, 21% refundable / 9% non-refundable in 2027, and 20% refundable / 10% non-refundable from 2028 onward.
Ontario, Alberta, British Columbia, Prairie, and Atlantic Regimes

In Ontario, the CRA administers two complementary corporate R&D credits that reduce the federal pool of deductible and qualified SR&ED expenditures: the Ontario Innovation Tax Credit (OITC), which provides an 8% refundable tax credit for SMEs, and the Ontario Research and Development Tax Credit (ORDTC), which provides a 3.5% non-refundable tax credit on eligible Ontario R&D expenditures. In British Columbia, corporations claim a 10% B.C. SR&ED tax credit on qualified B.C. expenditures, which is refundable for qualifying CCPCs.

In Alberta, which maintains Canada's lowest general corporate income tax rate at 8%, the provincial government delivers the Innovation Employment Grant (IEG) through the corporate tax system via AT1 Schedule 29 under the lead policy oversight of the Ministry of Technology and Innovation. Available for eligible R&D expenditures incurred in Alberta after December 31, 2020 that match federal SR&ED eligibility criteria, the IEG provides an 8% payment on eligible Alberta R&D spending up to the corporation's base level of spending—calculated as the corporation's average qualifying R&D spending over the preceding two years—and an enhanced 20% payment on eligible R&D spending exceeding that two-year base level, on up to $4,000,000 in annual R&D spending. The IEG phases out incrementally for firms with taxable capital between $10,000,000 and $50,000,000, and corporations with $50,000,000 or more in taxable capital are ineligible.

In Saskatchewan, Sections 63 to 63.4 of The Income Tax Act (Saskatchewan) govern the Saskatchewan Research and Development Tax Credit, claimed on Schedule 403 (T2SCH403) and reported on lines 645 (refundable) and 631 (non-refundable) of Schedule 5. Following historical rate changes (where the credit was 15% refundable between March 31, 2009 and April 1, 2012, and subsequently 10% with a $1 million annual maximum credit), eligible expenditures incurred after March 31, 2017 qualified CCPCs for a 10% refundable credit on the first $1,000,000 of eligible expenditures for tax years beginning before December 16, 2024, and on the first $2,000,000 of eligible expenditures for tax years beginning after December 15, 2024, with excess CCPC expenditures and non-CCPC claims earning a non-refundable credit (subject to a 3-year carryback, 10-year carryforward, and statutory renunciation rights). Under Saskatchewan's 2026–27 Budget enhancements, which introduced that $2,000,000 limit, eligible capital expenditures—including new machinery, equipment and related lease or rental costs—were also added to the credit base, while total refundable and non-refundable credits remain limited to $1,000,000 annually; the Budget estimates $41 million in tax credits claimed in 2026–27 by over 2,700 private companies.

In Manitoba, the CRA administers the Manitoba Research and Development Tax Credit via Schedule 380 (T2SCH380) and lines 606 and 613 of Schedule 5. Equal to 15% of eligible Manitoba R&D expenditures made after April 11, 2017 (down from 20% previously), one-half of the credit for in-house R&D is refundable (yielding an effective 7.5% refundable credit and 7.5% non-refundable credit), whereas R&D conducted under an eligible contract with an institute is fully refundable. Non-refundable Manitoba credits may be carried back 3 years and carried forward 20 taxation years, and a corporation may renounce the credit in whole or in part under subsection 7.3(7) of the Income Tax Act (Manitoba).

Across Atlantic Canada and Yukon, four jurisdictions provide a uniform 15% fully refundable R&D tax credit administered by the CRA. Nova Scotia offers a 15% fully refundable credit under Section 41 of the Income Tax Act (Nova Scotia) via Schedule 340 (T2SCH340) for corporations with a permanent establishment in Nova Scotia, subject to an 18-month filing deadline after the corporation's tax year-end, recapture rules that increase Nova Scotia tax otherwise payable, and a right to renounce on or before 6 months after tax year-end. New Brunswick provides a 15% fully refundable credit (increased from 10%) via Schedule 360 (T2SCH360). Newfoundland and Labrador provides a 15% fully refundable credit under Section 42 of the Income Tax Act (Newfoundland and Labrador) (claimed via Form T1129 for trusts and individuals or the corporate T2 schedule within 12 months after the filing due date) to corporations, individuals, trusts, and partnerships; uniquely, Newfoundland and Labrador eligible expenditures are not reduced by government or non-government assistance other than GST/HST input tax credits. Finally, Yukon provides a 15% fully refundable R&D tax credit on eligible expenditures incurred in the territory.
Inter-Jurisdictional Assistance Mechanics, Proxy Method Interactions, and Combined Recovery Rates
The Government Assistance Grind-Down Mechanism (ITA Paragraph 37(1)(d) and Subsection 127(18))

Under paragraph 37(1)(d) and subsections 127(18) to (20) of the federal ITA, provincial and territorial R&D tax credits constitute government assistance that reduces both the federal pool of deductible SR&ED expenditures and qualified SR&ED expenditures for federal ITC purposes. Consequently, when stacking a provincial R&D tax credit of rate p with a federal SR&ED ITC of rate f on the same qualifying expenditure base E, the provincial credit p × E reduces the federal qualified expenditure base to E × (1 − p), resulting in a net combined recovery rate governed by:
Net combined rate = p + f × (1 − p)

Because non-refundable provincial R&D credits (such as Ontario's 3.5% ORDTC, the non-refundable 7.5% half of Manitoba's credit, or the non-refundable tier of Saskatchewan's credit) reduce federal qualified expenditures under subsection 127(18) even when the claimant has no provincial tax payable, Ontario, Manitoba (under subsection 7.3(7) of the Manitoba Act), Saskatchewan, and Nova Scotia explicitly permit corporations to renounce their provincial R&D credits on or before the statutory deadline so as to preserve their 35% refundable federal ITC.
The Proxy Method (PPA) Provincial Assistance Trap (ITA Paragraph 12(1)(x) vs. Subsection 127(18))

A critical statutory interaction occurs when a claimant uses the federal Proxy Method and earns a provincial or territorial R&D tax credit that is calculated on a base that includes the notional 55% Prescribed Proxy Amount (PPA). As established in Section 4.5 of the CRA Assistance and Contract Payments Policy, the portion of a provincial or territorial R&D tax credit that relates to the PPA is not included in determining the amount of government assistance applied to reduce the subsection 37(1) pool of deductible SR&ED expenditures under paragraph 37(1)(d), because the PPA is a notional amount that is never included in the subsection 37(1) pool. Instead, under the proxy method, the portion of the provincial or territorial R&D tax credit attributable to the PPA must be included directly in the claimant's taxable income under paragraph 12(1)(x) of the ITA in the taxation year in which it is received. Conversely, when computing qualified SR&ED expenditures for the federal ITC under subsection 127(18) of the ITA, 100% of the provincial or territorial tax credit—including the portion attributable to the PPA—reduces qualified SR&ED expenditures in the current year regardless of whether the claimant uses the proxy or traditional method and regardless of whether the provincial credit is refundable or non-refundable.

In Quebec, while the CRA's published assistance policy historically listed four former Quebec R&D credits as government assistance and had not yet formally updated its list for the CRIC as of late 2026, Quebec R&D tax credits claimed on SR&ED expenditures reduce the federal SR&ED expenditure pool, lowering a Quebec SME's 65% nominal combined rate (35% federal + 30% Quebec) to a net effective recovery rate of approximately 54.5% to 60%. However, where a Quebec claimant earns the 30% or 20% CRIC on pre-commercialization activities that lie outside the federal subsection 248(1) definition of SR&ED, those pre-commercialization credits do not constitute assistance in respect of federal SR&ED.

body.text: Strategic Compliance and Audit Risk Mitigation Conclusions

The convergence of the March 26, 2026 federal SR&ED Royal Assent legislation and the March 25, 2025 Quebec CRIC consolidation necessitates a comprehensive recalibration of R&D tax compliance and audit defence protocols across Canada. First, corporations acquiring laboratory, prototyping, or computing equipment after December 15, 2024 must implement asset-level operating-time logs to substantiate whether each depreciable property satisfies the 90% or more All or Substantially All (ASA) threshold for 100% capital inclusion on line 390 of Form T661 (and disclosure of the 10 most expensive properties per project on lines 262 and 263) or falls within the more than 50% to less than 90% primary-use band for first-term and second-term Shared-Use Equipment (SUE) on line 504. Claimants with taxation years straddling December 16, 2024 must strictly segregate pre-December 16, 2024 capital acquisitions and lease payments from post-December 15, 2024 outlays across lines 390, 504, 514, 535, and 540.

Second, capital-intensive CCPCs whose prior-year taxable capital employed in Canada exceeds the newly increased $15,000,000 threshold should evaluate electing on the prescribed form to compute their enhanced expenditure limit under the ECPC three-year average annual revenue method pursuant to subsections 127(10.31) and 127(10.6) of the ITA, thereby preserving access to the 35% enhanced ITC on up to $6,000,000 of annual SR&ED spending. Publicly traded Canadian technology and life sciences companies must similarly verify their qualification as Eligible Canadian Public Corporations (ECPCs) throughout the taxation year to capture the 35% enhanced rate.

Third, in multi-jurisdictional filings, tax directors of loss-making CCPCs in Ontario, Manitoba, and Saskatchewan should model the statutory renunciation of non-refundable provincial credits (such as Ontario's 3.5% ORDTC or the non-refundable 7.5% portion of Manitoba's credit under subsection 7.3(7)) to prevent subsection 127(18) from eroding 35% cash-refundable federal ITCs, while ensuring that any provincial credit earned on the notional 55% PPA is excluded from the paragraph 37(1)(d) pool grind and recognized under paragraph 12(1)(x) only in the year received. In Quebec, businesses beginning fiscal periods after March 25, 2025 should establish dual-track project accounting that separates core SR&ED activities from downstream pre-commercialization and industrial design work under the 30%/20% CRIC, while ensuring that software teams transitioning from the CDAE to the CDAEIA after December 31, 2025 document significant artificial intelligence integration for Investissement Québec certification. Finally, all technical narratives on Form T661 should present projects globally across the taxation year in accordance with Les Abeilles Service de Conditionnement Inc. while demonstrating through contemporaneous engineering records and credible technical testimony why the underlying technological uncertainties could not be resolved through routine engineering under the five-question standard of Northwest Hydraulic Consultants Limited v. The Queen, C.W. Agencies Inc. v. The Queen, and Manning Canning Kitchens Inc. v. His Majesty the King.
